claim: The cerebellum contributes to a diverse array of motor conditions, including ataxia, dystonia, and tremor.
source: The cerebellum contributes to a diverse array of motor conditions, including ataxia, dystonia, and tremor.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a foundational premise of the study.

claim: The neural substrates that encode the diversity of cerebellar motor conditions are unclear.
source: The neural substrates that encode this diversity are unclear.
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the abstract as the knowledge gap the study addresses.

claim: A supervised classifier model can correctly assign mouse phenotypes based on single-neuron spike signatures.
source: The classifier model correctly assigned mouse phenotypes based on single-neuron signatures.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 1E.

claim: Spike signatures are shared across etiologically distinct but phenotypically similar disease models.
source: Spike signatures were shared across etiologically distinct but phenotypically similar disease models.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figures 2-4.

claim: Mimicking pathophysiological spike signatures with optogenetics induces predicted motor impairments in otherwise healthy mice.
source: Mimicking these pathophysiological spike signatures with optogenetics induced the predicted motor impairments in otherwise healthy mice.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: Distinct spike signatures promote the behavioral presentation of cerebellar diseases.
source: These data show that distinct spike signatures promote the behavioral presentation of cerebellar diseases.
evidence: This is the main conclusion stated in the abstract, synthesizing the findings.

claim: Patients with cerebellar lesions showed loss of precise motor coordination, referred to as ataxia.
source: Patients with various cerebellar lesions showed loss of precise motor coordination, which, as the consequence of disease, is referred to as ataxia, whereas some subjects displayed overt and sometimes exaggerated oscillatory movements, consistent with tremor (Holmes, 1917; Turner, 1892; Holmes, 1939).
evidence: This is supported by citations to historical studies by Holmes and Turner.

claim: Some patients with cerebellar lesions displayed oscillatory movements consistent with tremor.
source: Patients with various cerebellar lesions showed loss of precise motor coordination, which, as the consequence of disease, is referred to as ataxia, whereas some subjects displayed overt and sometimes exaggerated oscillatory movements, consistent with tremor (Holmes, 1917; Turner, 1892; Holmes, 1939).
evidence: This is supported by citations to historical studies by Holmes and Turner.

claim: Uncontrolled muscle contractions are a contributing feature of dystonia.
source: In other cases, the examiner would report uncontrolled muscle contractions, which is now a contributing feature of dystonia (Balint et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Balint et al., 2018.

claim: Loss of GABAergic neurotransmission from Purkinje cells causes uncoordinated movements and disequilibrium indicative of ataxia.
source: Loss of GABAergic neurotransmission from Purkinje cells, which provide the sole output of the cerebellar cortex, caused uncoordinated movements and disequilibrium that were indicative of ataxia (Figure 1A; White et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to White et al., 2014 and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Eliminating glutamatergic neurotransmission from climbing fibers causes twisting postures and hyperextended limbs consistent with dystonia.
source: In contrast, eliminating glutamatergic neurotransmission from climbing fibers, which synapse onto Purkinje cells, caused twisting postures and hyperextended limbs that are consistent with dystonia (Figure 1A; White and Sillitoe, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to White and Sillitoe, 2017 and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Systemic injection of harmaline causes hyperactivation of climbing fibers and rhythmic bursting spike activity in Purkinje cells as well as severe tremor.
source: In addition, systemic injection of the β-carboline alkaloid drug harmaline caused hyperactivation of climbing fibers and rhythmic bursting spike activity in Purkinje cells as well as a severe tremor (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Optogenetically modulating Purkinje cell projections to cerebellar nuclei cells in a bursting pattern induces oscillatory tremor movements.
source: Optogenetically modulating Purkinje cell projections to cerebellar nuclei cells in a bursting pattern induced oscillatory tremor movements (Stratton and Lorden, 1991; Brown et al., 2020b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Stratton and Lorden, 1991 and Brown et al., 2020b.

claim: The classifier model identified skewness as the best differentiator between neurons recorded in ataxic and control mice versus neurons recorded in dystonic and tremoring mice.
source: The classifier model identified 'skewness' (Figure 1D) as the best differentiator between neurons recorded in ataxic and control mice (lower skewness) and neurons recorded in dystonic and tremoring mice (higher skewness).
evidence: This is stated in the results and illustrated in Figure 1D.

claim: The classifier model identified CV2 as the best differentiator of neurons recorded in ataxic mice from control mice.
source: Next, the classifier model identified CV2 (Holt et al., 1996; Figure 1—figure supplement 1E) as the best differentiator of neurons recorded in ataxic mice (lower CV2) from control mice (higher CV2).
evidence: This is stated in the results and illustrated in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: The classifier model identified ISI>25 as the best differentiator of neurons from mice with tremor compared to those recorded in dystonic mice.
source: Last, the classifier model identified that the ISI>25 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C), which measures the percentage of ISI with a duration over 25 ms (or instantaneous firing rate under 40 Hz) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G), as the best differentiator of neurons from the mice with tremor (lower ISI>25) compared to those recorded in dystonic mice (higher ISI>25) (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and illustrated in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C, G.

claim: 85% of neurons recorded in control mice had a control signature.
source: We found that the classifier model indeed assigned the signature that aligned with different predominant phenotypes of each archetypal mouse model correctly for the majority of neurons (control: 85% of neurons recorded in a control mouse had a control signature; ataxia: 79%; dystonia: 88%; tremor: 54%) (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 1E.

claim: 79% of neurons recorded in ataxic mice had an ataxia signature.
source: We found that the classifier model indeed assigned the signature that aligned with different predominant phenotypes of each archetypal mouse model correctly for the majority of neurons (control: 85% of neurons recorded in a control mouse had a control signature; ataxia: 79%; dystonia: 88%; tremor: 54%) (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 1E.

claim: 88% of neurons recorded in dystonic mice had a dystonia signature.
source: We found that the classifier model indeed assigned the signature that aligned with different predominant phenotypes of each archetypal mouse model correctly for the majority of neurons (control: 85% of neurons recorded in a control mouse had a control signature; ataxia: 79%; dystonia: 88%; tremor: 54%) (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 1E.

claim: 54% of neurons recorded in tremor mice had a tremor signature.
source: We found that the classifier model indeed assigned the signature that aligned with different predominant phenotypes of each archetypal mouse model correctly for the majority of neurons (control: 85% of neurons recorded in a control mouse had a control signature; ataxia: 79%; dystonia: 88%; tremor: 54%) (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Most Atxn1154Q/+ neurons exhibited a control signature (22/34).
source: Despite the presence of an ataxic phenotype at this age (Supplementary file 1), we observed that most Atxn1154Q/+ neurons exhibited a control signature (22/34) and that the second most numerous spike train signature was a dystonia signature (10/24).
evidence: This is stated in the results section describing Atxn1154Q/+ mice.

claim: The second most numerous spike train signature in Atxn1154Q/+ mice was a dystonia signature (10/24).
source: Despite the presence of an ataxic phenotype at this age (Supplementary file 1), we observed that most Atxn1154Q/+ neurons exhibited a control signature (22/34) and that the second most numerous spike train signature was a dystonia signature (10/24).
evidence: This is stated in the results section describing Atxn1154Q/+ mice.

claim: Half of the neurons in Pcp2Cre;Ank1fl/fl mice exhibited an abnormal spike train signature, with the majority classified with the dystonia spike train signature (6/14).
source: In this mouse model, we found that half of the neurons exhibited an abnormal spike train signature, with the majority classified with the dystonia spike train signature (6/14).
evidence: This is stated in the results section describing Pcp2Cre;Ank1fl/fl mice.

claim: The population distribution of skewness values was lower in ataxic Atxn1154Q/+ (0.14 ± 0.02) and Pcp2Cre;Ank1fl/fl (0.17 ± 0.03) mouse models than in the archetypal dystonia model (0.42 ± 0.05).
source: Indeed, the population distribution of skewness values was lower in the ataxic Atxn1154Q/+ (0.14 ± 0.02 [mean ± SEM]) and Pcp2Cre;Ank1fl/fl (0.17 ± 0.03) mouse models (Figure 2D and E) than in our archetypal dystonia model (0.42 ± 0.05) (Ptf1aCre;Slc17a6fl/fl, Figure 1F and G).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figures 1F, G and 2D, E.

claim: The difference in skewness between Atxn1154Q/+ and Ptf1aCre;Slc17a6fl/fl mice was statistically significant (p<0.0001).
source: We used a one-way ANOVA followed by Tukey post hoc analyses and found that the difference in skewness between the ataxia models and the dystonia models was statistically significant (Atxn1154Q/+ vs. Ptf1aCre;Slc17a6fl/fl: p<0.0001; Pcp2Cre;Ank1fl/fl vs. Ptf1aCre;Slc17a6fl/fl: p = 0.0025), but we did not observe a difference in skewness between the two ataxia models (Atxn1154Q/+ vs. Pcp2Cre;Ank1fl/fl: p = 0.9961).
evidence: This is stated in the results with statistical test results.

claim: The difference in skewness between Pcp2Cre;Ank1fl/fl and Ptf1aCre;Slc17a6fl/fl mice was statistically significant (p = 0.0025).
source: We used a one-way ANOVA followed by Tukey post hoc analyses and found that the difference in skewness between the ataxia models and the dystonia models was statistically significant (Atxn1154Q/+ vs. Ptf1aCre;Slc17a6fl/fl: p<0.0001; Pcp2Cre;Ank1fl/fl vs. Ptf1aCre;Slc17a6fl/fl: p = 0.0025), but we did not observe a difference in skewness between the two ataxia models (Atxn1154Q/+ vs. Pcp2Cre;Ank1fl/fl: p = 0.9961).
evidence: This is stated in the results with statistical test results.

claim: There was no significant difference in skewness between Atxn1154Q/+ and Pcp2Cre;Ank1fl/fl mice (p = 0.9961).
source: We used a one-way ANOVA followed by Tukey post hoc analyses and found that the difference in skewness between the ataxia models and the dystonia models was statistically significant (Atxn1154Q/+ vs. Ptf1aCre;Slc17a6fl/fl: p<0.0001; Pcp2Cre;Ank1fl/fl vs. Ptf1aCre;Slc17a6fl/fl: p = 0.0025), but we did not observe a difference in skewness between the two ataxia models (Atxn1154Q/+ vs. Pcp2Cre;Ank1fl/fl: p = 0.9961).
evidence: This is stated in the results with statistical test results.

claim: Pdx1Cre;Slc17a6fl/fl mice exhibit mild dystonic symptoms only in response to a stressful event.
source: We included two dystonia models in our analyses; Pdx1Cre;Slc17a6fl/fl mice exhibit mild dystonic symptoms only in response to a stressful event (Lackey, 2021; Leon and Sillitoe, 2023; Figure 3A and B), whereas mice that receive ouabain applied to the surface of the cerebellum exhibit continuous severe dystonic features (Fremont et al., 2014; Calderon et al., 2011; Figure 3A and B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by citations to Lackey, 2021 and Leon and Sillitoe, 2023.

claim: Mice that receive ouabain applied to the surface of the cerebellum exhibit continuous severe dystonic features.
source: We included two dystonia models in our analyses; Pdx1Cre;Slc17a6fl/fl mice exhibit mild dystonic symptoms only in response to a stressful event (Lackey, 2021; Leon and Sillitoe, 2023; Figure 3A and B), whereas mice that receive ouabain applied to the surface of the cerebellum exhibit continuous severe dystonic features (Fremont et al., 2014; Calderon et al., 2011; Figure 3A and B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by citations to Fremont et al., 2014 and Calderon et al., 2011.

claim: The proportion of neurons with a control signature was greater in Pdx1Cre;Slc17a6fl/fl mice than in ouabain infusion mice (7/23 vs. 13/21, z = −2.094, p = 0.0366).
source: We found that the proportion of neurons that exhibited the control signature was greater in Pdx1Cre;Slc17a6fl/fl mice than in ouabain infusion mice (7/23 vs. 13/21, z = −2.094, p = 0.0366; Figure 3C).
evidence: This is stated in the results with statistical test results and shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The proportion of neurons with a dystonia signature was lower in Pdx1Cre;Slc17a6fl/fl mice than in ouabain infusion mice (15/23 vs. 7/21, z = 2.1128, p = 0.0349).
source: Moreover, the proportion of neurons with a dystonia signature was lower in Pdx1Cre;Slc17a6fl/fl mice than in ouabain infusion mice (15/23 vs. 7/21, z = 2.1128, p = 0.0349; Figure 3C).
evidence: This is stated in the results with statistical test results and shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The distribution of skewness values differed between Pdx1Cre;Slc17a6fl/fl (0.12 ± 0.05) and ouabain infusion mice (0.36 ± 0.8).
source: In addition to the proportional differences in cells with a control and dystonia signature, we found that the distribution of skewness values differed between the Pdx1Cre;Slc17a6fl/fl (0.12 ± 0.05) and ouabain infusion mice (0.36 ± 0.8) (Figure 3D and E).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figures 3D and E.

claim: Skewness was lower in Pdx1Cre;Slc17a6fl/fl mice with mild dystonic features compared to ouabain infusion mice (p = 0.0012).
source: We quantified this difference by comparing these two mouse models to each other and the archetypal dystonic model (Ptf1aCre;Slc17a6fl/fl) using a one-way ANOVA followed by Tukey post hoc analysis. We found that the skewness was lower in Pdx1Cre;Slc17a6fl/fl mice with mild dystonic features compared to the ouabain infusion mice (p = 0.0012) and Ptf1aCre;Slc17a6fl/fl mice (p<0.0001) with severe dystonic features.
evidence: This is stated in the results with statistical test results.

claim: Skewness was lower in Pdx1Cre;Slc17a6fl/fl mice with mild dystonic features compared to Ptf1aCre;Slc17a6fl/fl mice (p<0.0001) with severe dystonic features.
source: We quantified this difference by comparing these two mouse models to each other and the archetypal dystonic model (Ptf1aCre;Slc17a6fl/fl) using a one-way ANOVA followed by Tukey post hoc analysis. We found that the skewness was lower in Pdx1Cre;Slc17a6fl/fl mice with mild dystonic features compared to the ouabain infusion mice (p = 0.0012) and Ptf1aCre;Slc17a6fl/fl mice (p<0.0001) with severe dystonic features.
evidence: This is stated in the results with statistical test results.

claim: There was no significant difference in skewness between ouabain infusion mice and Ptf1aCre;Slc17a6fl/fl mice (p = 0.9274).
source: There was no significant difference between the two models with severe dystonic features (p = 0.9274).
evidence: This is stated in the results with statistical test results.

claim: Car8wdl/wdl mice exhibit a severe oscillatory tremor that can be reduced to control levels by treatment with propranolol.
source: We previously showed that Car8wdl/wdl mice exhibit a severe oscillatory tremor that can be reduced to control levels by treatment with the β-blocker drug propranolol (Zhou et al., 2022), which is used to treat tremor in human patients.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by citation to Zhou et al., 2022.

claim: Car8wdl/wdl mice exhibit ataxia and dystonia, which are not normalized by propranolol.
source: Car8wdl/wdl mice also exhibit ataxia and dystonia, which are not normalized by propranolol (Jiao et al., 2005; White et al., 2016a; Miterko et al., 2021; Zhou et al., 2022).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Before treatment, Car8wdl/wdl mice exhibited a large proportion of neurons with the tremor signature (8/13).
source: We found that, before treatment, Car8wdl/wdl mice exhibited a large proportion of neurons with the tremor signature (8/13).
evidence: This is stated in the results section describing Car8wdl/wdl mice.

claim: In propranolol-treated Car8wdl/wdl mice, the proportion of neurons with the tremor signature was diminished while control (6/15) and dystonia (6/15) signatures were the most common signatures.
source: However, in propranolol-treated Car8wdl/wdl mice the proportion of neurons with the tremor signature was diminished while control (6/15) and dystonia (6/15) signatures were the most common signatures (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 4C.

claim: There is a shift toward higher ISI>25 values in propranolol-treated Car8wdl/wdl mice compared to untreated Car8wdl/wdl mice.
source: The classifier model differentiates between the dystonia and tremor signature based on the ISI>25 value, and, indeed, we find a shift toward higher ISI>25 values in propranolol-treated Car8wdl/wdl mice compared to untreated Car8wdl/wdl mice (Figure 4D and E).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figures 4D and E.

claim: The ataxia stimulation paradigm induced cells to develop a response similar to the Atxn1154Q/+ and Pcp2Cre;Ank1fl/fl ataxia model mice, with about half of the cells remaining within the control signature (7/16), and half shifting into the dystonia signature (8/16).
source: We found that the ataxia stimulation paradigm induced cells to develop a response similar to the Atxn1154Q/+ and Pcp2Cre;Ank1fl/fl ataxia model mice (Figure 3, Figure 5—figure supplement 2), with about half of the cells remaining within the control signature (7/16), and half shifting into the dystonia signature (8/16) (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 5F and Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: The ataxia stimulation resulted in significantly lower skewness than the dystonia stimulation (p = 0.0287).
source: Also akin to these models, when we used a one-way ANOVA followed by Tukey post hoc analysis to compare the ataxia and dystonia stimulation responses, we found the ataxia stimulation resulted in significantly lower skewness than the dystonia stimulation (ataxia stimulation versus dystonia stimulation: p = 0.0287).
evidence: This is stated in the results with statistical test results.

claim: The dystonia stimulation induced the majority of cells to produce spike signatures that the classifier model defined as dystonic (9/16 cells).
source: Additionally, we found that the dystonia and tremor stimulation induced the majority of cells to produce spike signatures that our classifier model defined as dystonic (9/16 cells) or as tremor signatures (11/16 cells), respectively (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 5F.

claim: The tremor stimulation induced the majority of cells to produce tremor signatures (11/16 cells).
source: Additionally, we found that the dystonia and tremor stimulation induced the majority of cells to produce spike signatures that our classifier model defined as dystonic (9/16 cells) or as tremor signatures (11/16 cells), respectively (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Each optogenetic stimulation paradigm resulted in a different constellation of behaviors, with the ataxia stimulation paradigm resulting in imprecise movements, the dystonia stimulation paradigm resulting in prominent dystonic posturing, and the tremor stimulation paradigm resulting in severe tremor.
source: Changes in behavior were immediate and severe as soon as the stimulation began. Each stimulation paradigm resulted in a different constellation of behaviors, with the ataxia stimulation paradigm resulting in imprecise movements, the dystonia stimulation paradigm resulting in prominent dystonic posturing, and the tremor stimulation paradigm resulting in severe tremor (Video 3).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Video 3.

claim: All stimulation paradigms affected gait, resulting in visibly different foot placement and movement down the footprinting corridor.
source: We found that all stimulation paradigms affected gait, resulting in visibly different foot placement (Figure 6E-H) and movement down the footprinting corridor (Video 4).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figures 6E-H and Video 4.

claim: All stimulation paradigms resulted in shorter steps and less precision of fore and hindpaw placement.
source: Quantitatively, this was evident in shorter steps and less precision of fore and hindpaw placement (Figure 6I–K).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figures 6I-K.

claim: The dystonia stimulation paradigm resulted in the most frequent and strongest dystonic movements.
source: The dystonia stimulation paradigm resulted in the most frequent and strongest dystonic movements, while we also observed dystonic movements with the ataxia paradigm and abnormal movement – namely severe tremor – was noted with the tremor stimulation paradigm (Figure 6M).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 6M.

claim: The ataxia stimulation paradigm did not significantly increase tremor from baseline.
source: While the ataxia stimulation paradigm did not significantly increase tremor from baseline, both the dystonia and tremor stimulation paradigms resulted in a significantly increased tremor at 10 Hz (Figure 6N–P).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figures 6N-P.

claim: Both the dystonia and tremor stimulation paradigms resulted in a significantly increased tremor at 10 Hz.
source: While the ataxia stimulation paradigm did not significantly increase tremor from baseline, both the dystonia and tremor stimulation paradigms resulted in a significantly increased tremor at 10 Hz (Figure 6N–P).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figures 6N-P.

claim: The tremor paradigm resulted in the most severe tremor of all stimulation conditions, producing a tremor severity that was more than tenfold greater than that of the dystonia stimulation paradigm.
source: Indeed, the tremor paradigm resulted in the most severe tremor of all stimulation conditions, producing a tremor severity that was more than tenfold greater than that of the dystonia stimulation paradigm.
evidence: This is stated in the results section describing tremor measurements.

claim: All three stimulation parameters resulted in a behavioral repertoire that was significantly different from baseline.
source: Together, these measurements produced a complex representation of the underlying phenotypes. All three stimulation parameters resulted in a behavioral repertoire that was significantly different from baseline and, while there was some overlap of features, each stimulation paradigm produced the distinct and predicted respective motor phenotype (Figure 6Q–T).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figures 6Q-T.

claim: Each stimulation paradigm produced the distinct and predicted respective motor phenotype.
source: Together, these measurements produced a complex representation of the underlying phenotypes. All three stimulation parameters resulted in a behavioral repertoire that was significantly different from baseline and, while there was some overlap of features, each stimulation paradigm produced the distinct and predicted respective motor phenotype (Figure 6Q–T).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figures 6Q-T.

claim: The classifier model's defined spike signatures of disease-associated cerebellar nuclei spike trains are sufficient to produce the predicted corresponding abnormal motor phenotypes in mice.
source: Together these data suggest that our classifier model's defined spike signatures of disease-associated cerebellar nuclei spike trains are sufficient to produce the predicted corresponding abnormal motor phenotypes in mice.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results section.

claim: Degenerative ataxias and non-degenerative ataxias may have different underlying circuit alterations that lead to distinct spike signatures.
source: Therefore, our work suggests that degenerative ataxias and non-degenerative ataxias may have different underlying circuit alterations that lead to distinct spike signatures.
evidence: This is an interpretation stated in the discussion based on the observed differences between ataxia models.

claim: There is a healthy range within the characteristics of cerebellar nuclei spiking activity and cerebellar movement disorders are associated with a shift from this range in one or multiple features of spike train activity.
source: Our work suggests that there is a healthy range within the characteristics of cerebellar nuclei spiking activity and that cerebellar movement disorders are associated with a shift from this range in one or multiple features of spike train activity.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the discussion.

claim: Pathophysiological spike train signatures are driven by a shift in neural function toward a disease state that can be independent of plasticity or circuit rewiring.
source: These findings suggest that pathophysiological spike train signatures are driven by a shift in neural function toward a disease state that can be independent of plasticity or circuit rewiring.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the discussion.

claim: Co-expression or comorbidity of different motor disease behaviors may arise due to a spectrum of spike signal defects.
source: Despite the dramatically different behavioral outcomes, the potential overlap and shared spike features, such as the irregular spike pattern found in the dystonia and tremor signatures, raise the strong possibility that co-expression or comorbidity of different motor disease behaviors may arise due to a spectrum of spike signal defects.
evidence: This is an interpretation stated in the discussion based on observed overlap in spike features.

claim: It is possible for neural signals to shift back and forth between healthy and disease states, potentially resulting in the transientness of behavioral impairments in certain cerebellar disorders.
source: This indicates that it is possible for neural signals to shift back and forth between healthy and disease states, potentially resulting in the transientness of behavioral impairments in certain cerebellar disorders.
evidence: This is an interpretation stated in the discussion based on the findings.

claim: The most successful therapeutic avenues for cerebellar movement disorders should maintain cerebellar spiking activity within the healthy range without inadvertently inducing a different pathophysiological signature.
source: These findings also suggest that the most successful therapeutic avenues for cerebellar movement disorders should maintain cerebellar spiking activity within the healthy range without inadvertently inducing a different pathophysiological signature.
evidence: This is a recommendation stated in the discussion based on the findings.

claim: Recordings of nuclei cells are more likely to be from excitatory neurons because excitatory nuclei cells are larger than inhibitory nuclei cells.
source: We can speculate that, as excitatory nuclei cells are larger than inhibitory nuclei cells (Uusisaari et al., 2007), our recordings of nuclei cells are more likely to be from excitatory neurons.
evidence: This is speculation stated in the discussion and supported by citation to Uusisaari et al., 2007.

claim: The optogenetic technique uses Purkinje cell terminals to modulate nuclei activity and therefore would impact both excitatory and inhibitory nuclei neurons.
source: However, our optogenetic technique uses Purkinje cell terminals to modulate nuclei activity and therefore would impact both excitatory and inhibitory nuclei neurons (Canto et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by citation to Canto et al., 2016.

claim: Recordings in human patients during DBS implantation have previously found physiological differences in the spike train patterns of basal ganglia neurons between dystonia and other movement disorders.
source: Recordings in human patients during DBS implantation have previously found physiological differences in the spike train patterns of basal ganglia neurons between dystonia and other movement disorders (e.g., etiologically distinct dystonia: McClelland et al., 2016; dystonia with and without head tremor: Sedov et al., 2020; dystonia versus Parkinson's disease: Tang et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Nonsimultaneous recordings from a population of heterogeneous neurons are sufficient to determine distinct pathogenic signatures among the variability of the dataset.
source: Here we show that these nonsimultaneous recordings from a population of heterogeneous neurons are sufficient to determine distinct pathogenic signatures among the variability of our dataset.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the discussion based on the study's findings.

claim: The electrophysiological data confirm that differences between disease presentations are found in the spike train properties of the cerebellum.
source: Our electrophysiological data confirm that differences between disease presentations are found in the spike train properties of the cerebellum and our optogenetic experiments suggest that these spike trains are not merely biomarkers that correlate with the disease state but are sufficient to cause motor impairments.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the discussion based on the study's findings.

claim: The optogenetic experiments suggest that spike trains are not merely biomarkers that correlate with the disease state but are sufficient to cause motor impairments.
source: Our electrophysiological data confirm that differences between disease presentations are found in the spike train properties of the cerebellum and our optogenetic experiments suggest that these spike trains are not merely biomarkers that correlate with the disease state but are sufficient to cause motor impairments.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the discussion based on the study's findings.

claim: Cerebellar-targeted DBS may be highly beneficial in normalizing disease-causing spike train patterns.
source: Therefore, it is not clear whether our model would become stronger by considering both cerebellar activity and activity elsewhere in the motor circuit or whether considering multiple areas would be redundant. Our previous work and what we have shown here suggest cerebellar-targeted DBS may be highly beneficial in normalizing disease-causing spike train patterns.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the discussion based on the study's findings.

claim: Incorrect modulation of nuclei activity in neurodegenerative ataxias or lack of correct modulation in Pcp2Cre;Slc32a1fl/fl ataxia may lead to the ataxia phenotype.
source: Modulation of interposed nucleus activity alters movement trajectories (Becker and Person, 2019). Therefore, incorrect modulation of nuclei activity in the neurodegenerative ataxias or lack of correct modulation in Pcp2Cre;Slc32a1fl/fl ataxia may lead to the ataxia phenotype.
evidence: This is an interpretation stated in the discussion and supported by citation to Becker and Person, 2019.

claim: The suppressed periods of the irregular pattern associated with dystonia may be related to the timing of dystonic muscle contractions.
source: The dystonic models herein were characterized with irregular and slow firing. Previous work has associated bursts of Purkinje cell activity with dystonic postures (Hisatsune et al., 2013), and therefore, the suppressed periods of the irregular pattern associated with dystonia may be related to the timing of dystonic muscle contractions.
evidence: This is an interpretation stated in the discussion and supported by citation to Hisatsune et al., 2013.

claim: Stimulation of Purkinje cell terminals in the cerebellar nuclei, resulting in suppression of cerebellar nuclei activity, directly precedes muscle contractions.
source: Indeed, in our previous work we have shown that stimulation of Purkinje cell terminals in the cerebellar nuclei, resulting in suppression of cerebellar nuclei activity, directly precedes muscle contractions (Brown et al., 2020b).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by citation to Brown et al., 2020b.

claim: A large proportion of the population of neurons must produce the abnormal spike signature in order to produce a severe motor phenotype.
source: For all phenotypes, we expect that a large proportion of the population of neurons must produce the abnormal spike signature in order to produce a severe motor phenotype (Figures 2 and 3).
evidence: This is an interpretation stated in the discussion based on data in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: The optogenetic behavioral studies likely induced synchrony of both Purkinje and nuclei cell activity in addition to the intended spike signature.
source: Our optogenetic behavioral studies likely induced synchrony of both Purkinje and nuclei cell activity in addition to the intended spike signature; therefore, our work here supports synchronous abnormal firing for the phenotypes we produced.
evidence: This is an interpretation stated in the discussion.
